About

Created for law enforcement. Kept going by education.

Namaste Equine Rescue was created in 2014 to originally help law enforcement that had seized equines. What we found in the years since changed what this place is for.

The mission, in full

To procure equines seized by law enforcement, primarily serving the state of Wisconsin, to rehabilitate them mentally and physically and re-home them in a safe, forever environment.

Shelter, food, vet and farrier care, and unconditional attention. Four things that sound simple written down, and are the entire budget and the entire calendar.

We also commit to educating law enforcement and owners on proper management, to further protect equines in this state.

What we learned

99% of our purpose was to educate horse owners.

We started out expecting to be a destination — the barn at the end of a bad situation. What became obvious was that most of these cases were not malice. They were owners in over their heads, and nobody had ever shown them what a healthy horse looks like.

So the work turned into education. The horse still gets rehabilitated — but the owner learns something, the department learns something, and sometimes the next horse never gets seized at all.

Learn

Ninety-nine percent of this job is teaching people to read a horse.

That is not a slogan, it is what this rescue found out. Most neglect cases are not malice — they are an owner who never learned what a healthy horse feels like under the hand. So here is the thing we actually want you to take away from this website.

The Henneke scale

Score a horse in six places.

Body condition is not a guess and it is not a look. It is six places you put your hands, each scored one to nine, then averaged. The six places are marked here on Captain, a horse who came through this farm. What each of the nine scores looks like is further down the page.

Captain · the six places, on a real horse
5 · Moderate Dashed · where an ideal 5 would sit

What this is. A horse that is too thin cannot tell you. So you check it with your hands, in six particular places, and give each place a number from 1 to 9. Low numbers mean too thin. High numbers mean too fat. Around 5 is right.

There are two sets of numbers here, and they are not the same thing. 1–6 on Captain are the six places you put your hands. 1–9 below are the nine scores — how much cover you find when you get there.

Choose a score · 1 to 9

1–3 · neglect range 4–6 · healthy 7–9 · over

What your hand is pressing through

A score is a feel, not a look.

Relative depths, drawn to show the idea rather than to measure it. Fat is the only layer that changes: the bone stays exactly where it was, which is why a hand on the same six places tells you the truth about a horse when your eye will not.

The whole scale on one line

Nine horses. One animal.

The very same photograph of Captain, nine times over, reshaped each time to show what that score looks like on a real horse. The one in the middle is his true photograph, untouched. Print this row for the barn wall, or tap any one of them.

See the difference

Two photographs of the same horse. The left one is the score you picked, the right one is a healthy horse.

    The dashed line on the left is where the healthy horse sits, laid over the one you picked. Same animal, same outline — only condition moved.

    Take it with you

    A one-page chart for the barn wall.

    All nine scores and all six places, on one sheet, in a table you can hold in one hand while the other one is on a horse. It prints from this page — no signup needed.

    Or have it sent

    Not connected in this concept — nothing is sent and no address is stored. On the live site this is the one thing on the website that turns a visitor into someone you can reach again.

    Now do it yourself

    Score a horse.

    Put a hand on all six places and give each one a number from one to nine. Do not average as you go and do not let one bad patch decide it — score each place on its own, then let the six of them settle it.

    What we ask of a foster home

    Never below a 4.

    Every horse placed with a Namaste foster home has to be kept at a minimum of 4 on this scale, monitored daily and written down. That number is on our foster agreement, and now you know exactly what it means.

    Foster requirements

    The scale was developed by Don Henneke at Texas A&M University and first published in 1983. It is scored by sight and by hand — a winter coat hides a great deal, which is why January cases are so often missed. Score all six areas separately and average them; one thin patch is not a thin horse.

    This page is here to teach, not to diagnose. If a horse you own scores 3 or below, that is a veterinary call, today — not a feeding decision you make on your own.

    The part everybody gets wrong

    You cannot just feed a starved horse.

    This is the single most useful thing on this website. The instinct — put food in front of it — is the instinct that kills. Reintroducing feed too fast triggers refeeding syndrome: insulin drives minerals and electrolytes out of the bloodstream and the horse can go down with edema, diarrhea, neurological signs or heart failure. It does not come from one meal. It builds over the first days to a week, right when everybody thinks the rescue is going well.

    Days 1–3

    One pound of alfalfa, every four hours

    Six small feeds a day, roughly half of what the horse actually needs. No grain at all. Good leafy alfalfa, because it produces a lower glucose and insulin response than grain or grass — which is precisely what you are trying to avoid.

    Days 4–5

    Two to three pounds, every four hours

    Still six feeds. Still no grain. About three quarters of requirement.

    Days 6–10

    Four to five pounds, every four hours

    Full requirement, and the feeds start consolidating toward three a day.

    Day 10 onward

    Slowly, for months

    Hay every eight to twelve hours, increasing gradually. Grain is not introduced until body condition has come up off the floor, and then in half-pound meals.

    1 in 5
    Emaciated horses that die during refeeding
    3–10 months
    To bring body condition back
    +250 lb
    What Red had to put back on

    Protocol as published from the refeeding trials run at UC Davis with rescue groups, and reproduced across equine nutrition guidance since. It is here so you understand why a starved horse needs a vet and a plan rather than a full hay net — not so you can run it yourself.

    What to do

    If a horse near you scores a 3 or below.

    If it is not your horse

    Call your county sheriff.

    Not us, first. We cannot seize a horse and neither can you — only law enforcement has that authority. Report it to them, in writing if you can, with the date and what you saw. Once a department has taken the animal, that is the point where this farm can step in.

    Write the report

    For law enforcement

    You have a seized equine and nowhere to put it tonight.

    That is the call this rescue exists to take. Tell us the county, the condition and how many. We will tell you straight away whether we have space, and we will open a file the moment the trailer arrives — the same file that follows the horse to its adopter.

    (262) 492-0767 What we need from you

    Adopt

    Do you have the perfect home for these animals?

    Applying does not obligate you to adopt an equine, and you do not need to have a particular horse in mind. Start the file, and we will talk.

    Start an adoption application See who is available

    Before you apply

    What we need to see.

    None of this is about wealth. It is about whether the horse in front of you will be safe, fed, and looked at every single day.

    • Prior experience owning equines.
    • At least 18 years old.
    • Living in Wisconsin or nearby. Out-of-state cases are evaluated individually.
    • Boarding at an approved facility, or keeping the animal on your own property.
    • A barn or a lean-to, safe and proper fencing — board or wire mesh is appropriate, no barbed wire.
    • Adequate water and feed supply.
    • Contact details for your veterinarian, farrier, and caregiver.
    • Willingness to let a Namaste representative visit before approval.

    The process

    Four steps, at the horse's pace.

    Start the application

    Work down what we need to see and send it. You do not have to name a horse, and a “not yet” on any line is a conversation rather than a refusal.

    We talk, and we visit

    A representative visits before any approval. Fencing, shelter, water, and where the horse would stand on a bad February night.

    You receive the file

    How the animal came to be here, the veterinary care it had, and what the staff noticed about it.

    We stay in touch, for good

    Periodic checks for the lifetime of the horse. Adopted animals cannot be moved on, leased or loaned without our approval.

    Questions we get

    Is there an adoption fee?

    Fees are handled case by case — ask us when you submit your application and we will be straight with you about what this particular horse has cost to bring back.

    I have never adopted a rescue horse. Am I out?

    No. We ask for prior equine ownership experience, not prior rescue experience. What matters is that you can read a horse and keep a routine.

    Why the lifetime check-ins?

    Because most of these animals were failed once already. The follow-up is not distrust of you; it is the promise we made to the horse.

    Can I adopt from out of state?

    Possibly. We serve Wisconsin primarily, and out-of-state applications are evaluated individually.

    Foster

    Give a horse a room while it gets its life back.

    Fostering is the difference between saying yes to a department and saying we have no space. You do not need to pick a horse first — apply, and we match the equine to your property, your abilities, and the care it needs.

    Start a foster application

    You provide

    The home and the daily work

    • Housing, hay, grain and shavings
    • Farrier work and routine vet checkups
    • Worming and any boarding fees
    • Feeding two to three times daily, with health monitoring

    We cover

    The veterinary side

    All veterinary costs except routine checkups, provided you use an approved vet. Non-emergency work needs board pre-approval.

    Emergency protocol

    In a life-threatening situation, a foster home may authorize care up to $350 without prior approval — then notify us immediately.

    The standard of care

    What we ask of every foster barn.

    These are not suggestions. They are the conditions the horse was taken away from somewhere else for lacking.

    Body condition

    Minimum 4 on the Henneke scale

    Monitored daily and written down.

    Forage

    Hay available 24/7

    Plus clean water at all times, and shelter from extreme weather.

    Fencing

    Capped t-posts, no barbed wire

    Safe fencing throughout. This one is non-negotiable.

    Feet

    Checked daily, trimmed every 6–8 weeks

    On schedule. Most intakes arrive years overdue.

    Worming

    Every three months

    On the rotation we agree with you at placement.

    Viewings

    Available for adoption visits

    With Namaste staff present. The goal is always the permanent home.

    Eligibility

    Within two hours of Union Grove.

    You will need experience owning equines, and the time, means and adequate facilities to care for one properly. Distance matters because we need to be able to reach you, and you need to be able to reach our vet.

    Start a foster application

    Volunteer

    Do you have the time to donate?

    We are looking for outgoing volunteers who are willing to commit their time here. An extra set of hands is always needed — and right now, with the facility being updated, that is more true than usual.

    Let's talk

    What the days look like

    Barn work, property work, and fundraising.

    Feeding and turnout. Stalls and water. Fencing, shelter repairs and the general business of keeping a farm standing through a Wisconsin winter. Alongside that, help with fundraising events is genuinely as valuable as an afternoon of mucking out.

    The current site does not publish a task list or a minimum commitment. Rather than invent one, this concept describes the work in general terms — the real rota is worth writing down and adding here.

    Bringing family

    Ages and supervision

    Under 14
    Direct parent or guardian supervision, working alongside them at all times.
    14 – 17
    Must be supervised by an adult.
    Parents
    Responsible for confirming that adult supervision is available before the visit.

    How to start

    Submit a volunteer application form, or simply get in touch and talk to us first. Most people do the second one.

    Get in touch

    Five horses

    Can you tell if a horse is hungry?

    Most people cannot, and that is the whole problem — neglect usually is not cruelty, it is an owner who never learned what a healthy horse looks like. Five horses, one guess each. It takes about a minute and you will not forget it afterwards.

    For law enforcement

    You have a seized equine and nowhere to put it tonight.

    That is the call this rescue was created to take. This page is written for the officer standing in the field, not for donors. It is short on purpose.

    Call the farm, any hour

    (262) 492-0767

    We will tell you straight away whether we have space. If we do not, say so and we will start ringing the barns we know.

    Have these four ready

    1. Which county, and the nearest town.
    2. How many animals, and roughly what size — pony, horse, draft.
    3. What condition they are in. A guess is fine. “Ribs showing” is enough.
    4. Whether they are safe where they stand right now, or need moving tonight.

    Before anything else

    Do not feed it up.

    This is the one thing worth knowing before we arrive. A starved horse given free access to feed can die of it. Reintroducing food too fast triggers refeeding syndrome: insulin drives minerals out of the bloodstream and the animal can go down with edema, diarrhea, neurological signs or heart failure. It builds over the first days to a week — right when everyone thinks it is going well. Roughly one emaciated horse in five is lost this way.

    Water, yes. A small amount of grass hay, yes. A full hay net or any grain, no. If the animal is staying put overnight, ring us and we will talk whoever is feeding it through the first three days.

    The refeeding protocol in full

    What happens next

    The moment the trailer arrives, a file opens.

    At intake

    Condition, recorded

    Body condition scored on the Henneke scale in six places, photographed, and written down with the date. Weight deficit, hydration, feet, skin, and anything else the animal arrived with.

    Through recovery

    A written record

    Veterinary and farrier work, the refeeding plan and how it was followed, and condition re-scored as it comes back. Red went from 250 lb underweight to placed; Captain took well over a year.

    Afterwards

    It follows the horse

    The file goes to the adopter, and a representative may check on the animal for the rest of its life. Adopted equines cannot be sold on, leased or loaned without our approval.

    Departments needing that record for a case should say so when they call. What the rescue can commit to providing, and in what form, is a question for the board rather than something this concept should invent.

    Straight answers

    What we cannot do.

    • We cannot seize an animal. Only your department can. We have no authority on anyone's property and we will not attend as though we do.
    • We cannot take an animal without a department involved. That is what separates this from a private surrender, and it is what protects the horse's status.
    • We cannot promise space. We can promise a straight answer within the length of a phone call, which is usually what you actually need.

    The farm

    Union Grove, Wisconsin.

    1904 51st Drive
    Union Grove, WI 53182

    Trailer access to the barn. Ring before you set off — we will meet you and take the animal straight in rather than leaving it standing in a yard.

    If you are worried about a horse

    Write it down, then make the call.

    Most neglect goes unreported because people are not sure, or they are not sure who to tell. Here is the whole of it: check what you are looking at, write down what you saw, and ring your county sheriff. You do not have to be certain, and you do not have to give your name.

    01

    Be sure what you are seeing

    A horse can look rough in February and be perfectly well. The six places tell you the difference in about two minutes. A score of 3 or below is the line.

    Score the horse first
    02

    Write down what you saw

    Dates, places and plain observations are what let a department act. Guesses and opinions are not. Fill the note below and it writes the report for you.

    03

    Ring your county sheriff

    Not us first. We cannot seize a horse and neither can you — only law enforcement has that authority. Once a department has taken the animal, that is the point where this farm can step in.

    The note

    What you saw, in the form a department can use.

    Nothing here leaves your browser. Fill in what you know, leave the rest blank, and copy the result into an email or read it down the phone.

       straight out of this rescue's own files — the intake header, the weight a horse had
       to put back on, the three things that actually save one.
    
  
    

  
    
    
    
      
      
    
        
    100% of every order goes back to the horses.
    
        
    Not "a portion of proceeds". After the cost of making the item, everything left
           goes to hay, farrier work, and veterinary bills for the next intake.
    
      
    
    
    
  
    

  
    
    
    

    
    
      
    Why merchandise
    Steady money, not just appeal money
    Donations spike after a bad case and then go quiet. Hay does not. A shop gives supporters a reason to give in the months when nothing dramatic is happening.
    
      
    Why these five
    A $12 way in and a $58 way in
    Someone who will never drive to Union Grove can still put a sticker on a tack box. The range matters more than any single item.
    
      
    Why the numbers
    Real records, not slogans
    Every graphic here is a fact from this rescue's own files. People ask what "+250" means, and then they get told about Red.
    
    
    

    
    This shop is a proposal. Nothing on
      these pages is connected to a payment system, no order can be placed, and the
      "100% to the horses" promise is a commitment for the board to approve — not an existing policy.
